fields.sections.0.h: Crisis marketing and exploitation of urgency
fields.sections.1.h: Same pattern of discount coupons and signup incentives
fields.sections.2.h: Cookie policy and legal coercion vicious cycle
fields.sections.0.ko: The author points out the practice of modern websites converting external crisis situations into marketing means. When major events like COVID-19 occur, most sites place related messages, but this amounts to mechanical response rather than actual information provision. Despite the low likelihood that users will read that content, companies repeat this to appear to express social responsibility.
fields.sections.1.ko: All websites use nearly identical discount offer formats. Structures like "10% off, email signup" have become elements users now expect as a matter of course, and each site repeats templates with verified high conversion rates instead of developing original incentives. This reveals that the entire web ecosystem is pursuing the same user experience formula.
fields.sections.2.ko: Regulations from the EU and California have forced all websites to publish cookie consent banners. The problem is that each site implements this in its own way, so users face different interfaces each time, making unified settings at the browser level impossible. The author argues this actually resulted in restricting user choice, and regardless of regulatory intent, only consistent forced consent methods from platforms have spread.
fields.caveat: An essay written in 2020, it does not reflect changes in the current web environment (AI content generation, new regulations, platform fragmentation, etc.), and as it is based on the author's subjective observation, it is not academic analysis backed by quantitative data.
